2️⃣ Crime Analysis in Los Angeles (2020–2023): A Data Analytics Case Study¶

  • Author: Andreza Eufrasio

  • Tools: Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn

    • File: data/crimes.csv

  • Dataset Source: DataCamp (educational)

  • Description:

This dataset contains reported crime incidents in Los Angeles from January 1, 2020 to July 3, 2023. Each record represents a single crime event and includes information about the type of crime, location, date and time of occurrence, and victim characteristics such as age, gender, and descent.

The dataset also provides details on weapon involvement and reporting information, enabling analysis of crime patterns across time, geography, and demographics.

This version of the dataset has been adapted for educational purposes from the original Los Angeles Open Data portal.

It supports exploratory and statistical analysis of crime trends, providing insights into high-risk areas, temporal patterns, and victim demographics.

3️⃣ Introduction¶

Los Angeles, California 🌴 — often known as the “City of Angels” and a global hub for entertainment — is one of the largest and most dynamic cities in the United States.

With its large population and geographic diversity, Los Angeles experiences a wide range of criminal activity. Understanding these patterns is essential for improving public safety and optimizing resource allocation.

In this case study, you have been tasked with supporting the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) by analyzing crime data to identify key trends in criminal behavior. The goal is to generate actionable insights that can support data-driven decision-making, enabling more effective allocation of police resources and targeted crime prevention strategies.

4️⃣ Objective:¶

Analyze crime patterns in Los Angeles between January 1, 2020 and July 3, 2023, with a focus on:

  • identifying the most common crime types
  • analyzing areas with the highest crime frequency
  • examining temporal patterns (hour, weekday vs weekend)
  • exploring victim demographics
  • assessing weapon involvement

5️⃣ The Data¶

They have provided you with a single dataset to use. A summary and preview are provided below.

Data Dictionary: crimes¶

File: crimes.csv¶

Column Type Description
dr_no integer Division of Records Number: official file number composed of year, area ID, and unique digits.
date_rptd datetime Date the crime was reported.
date_occ datetime Date the crime occurred.
time_occ datetime Time the crime occurred, converted from 24-hour format.
area_name string Geographic area or patrol division responsible for the incident.
crm_cd_desc string Description of the crime committed.
vict_age integer Victim's age in years.
vict_sex string Victim's sex (F = Female, M = Male, X = Unknown).
vict_descent string Victim's descent code.
weapon_desc string Description of the weapon used, if applicable.
status_desc string Status of the crime report.
location string Street address of the incident.

Derived Columns(Engineered Features)¶

Column Type Description
year integer Year extracted from date_occ.
month integer Month extracted from date_occ.
month_name string Month name extracted from date_occ.
day_of_week string Day of the week extracted from date_occ.
hour integer Hour extracted from time_occ for time-based analysis.
minute integer Minute extracted from time_occ.
time time/object Time component extracted from time_occ for precise time comparisons.
age_group category Victim age grouped into categories: 0–17, 18–25, 26–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, 65+.
weapon_used boolean Indicates whether a weapon was involved (True if weapon_desc is not missing, otherwise False).

Note: Derived features were created to support temporal, demographic, and behavioral analysis of crime patterns.

Handling Placeholder Values in Categorical Columns¶

Some categorical columns contain placeholder values (e.g., "?", "N/A", "unknown") that represent missing or invalid data. These values are not automatically recognized as missing by pandas and must be explicitly identified and handled.

In [663]:
# Common placeholders representing missing or invalid categorical values
bad_values = ["?", "N/A", "NA", "n/a", "unknown", "Unkonwn", "None", "", " ", "-", "--"]


# 2. Detect placeholder values in categorical columns
for col in crimes.select_dtypes(include=["object", "string", "category"]).columns:
    
    mask = crimes[col].isin(bad_values)
    bad_counts = mask.sum()

    if bad_counts > 0:
        print(f"⚠️ Column: '{col}' has {bad_counts} placeholder values\n")
        print(crimes.loc[mask].head(10), "\n")

#    else:
#        print(f"✅ Column: '{col}' has zero placeholder values from the defined list\n")

Date Formatting¶

In [670]:
crimes["date_rptd"] = pd.to_datetime(crimes["date_rptd"])
crimes["date_occ"]  = pd.to_datetime(crimes["date_occ"])

The date_rptd and date_occ columns are converted to datetime format to enable time-based analysis such as extracting the year, month, or weekday.

Time Formatting¶

Convert time_occ to a proper datetime format by preserving leading zeros and parsing it using the %H%M format. This ensures accurate extraction of hour and minute components for time-based analysis.

In [677]:
# Ensure all times have 4 digits
crimes["time_occ"] = crimes["time_occ"].str.zfill(4) 
# crimes["time_occ"].dt.strftime("%H:%M")             

# datetime operations
# This converts strings like "1110" into a real datetime format: 1900-01-01 11:10:00
crimes["time_occ"] = pd.to_datetime(crimes["time_occ"], format= "%H%M")

Feature Engineering¶

Create new features from date and time variables to support temporal analysis, including year, month, day of week, and hour.

In [684]:
crimes["year"] = crimes["date_occ"].dt.year
crimes["month"] = crimes["date_occ"].dt.month
crimes["month_name"] = crimes["date_occ"].dt.month_name()
crimes["day_of_week"] = crimes["date_occ"].dt.day_name()

From time_occ: hour

In [687]:
# .dt.hour - pandas extracts only the hour.
# .dt.hour - (represents full hour interval) You are grouping time into hourly buckets: 3 → all times between 3:00 and 3:59. No need to check minutes separately.

crimes["hour"] = crimes["time_occ"].dt.hour # type: integer. hour = 3 includes all times from 3:00 to 3:59



# .dt.minute - separate time into hour and minute for example: 11:10:00 → 10. This is useful if you need more precision.
crimes["minute"] = crimes["time_occ"].dt.minute


# .dt.time -  you extract only the time part. For example: 1900-01-01 11:10:00 → 11:10:00
# This is not string.
# It is also not pandas datetime64.
# It is a Python datetime.time object.
# That does not mean it is string.
# Compare precise time
crimes["time"] = crimes["time_occ"].dt.time  # type: datetime.time , But pandas stores Python objects in a column with dtype: object


# Good for display, plots, labels "11:10"
# Converts datetime → string format : 1900-01-01 11:10:00  → "11:10"
crimes["time_hm"] = crimes["time_occ"].dt.strftime("%H:%M")

Feature engineering enables more detailed analysis of crime patterns by time, allowing us to identify trends across hours, days, and months. These derived variables are essential for answering key analytical questions in this study.

Q1) Which hour has the highest frequency of crimes?¶

In [692]:
# value_counts() - Counts how many crimes occurred in each hour.
# idxmax() - Returns the index (hour) with the largest count. (type: integer)
#            Note: This method Returns the first occurrence in case of ties

peak_crime_hour = crimes["hour"].value_counts().idxmax()
peak_crime_hour
Out[692]:
12

The result confirms that 12 PM is the hour with the highest crime frequency.

Visualization Using Seaborn.countplot() - Using Dataframe — Crime Frequency by Hour¶

This visualization shows the number of crimes at each hour of the day, helping identify peak periods of criminal activity.

In [699]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))

sns.countplot(data=crimes, x="hour", color="steelblue")

plt.title("Crime Frequency by Hour of the Day", fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel("Hour of Day")
plt.ylabel("Number of Crimes")
plt.show()

Insight: Crime frequency peaks at 12 PM (noon), indicating a higher concentration of incidents during midday hours. Crime levels are lowest during early morning hours (approximately 2 AM to 5 AM), suggesting reduced activity when fewer people are active.

This pattern highlights a clear daily trend: crime increases throughout the morning, peaks at midday, and gradually declines in the evening. This insight can support resource allocation by identifying periods of increased crime activity.

Q2) Which area has the highest frequency of night crimes (10 PM–3:59 AM)?¶

In [702]:
# .dt.hour - (represents full hour interval) You are grouping time into hourly buckets: 3 → all times between 3:00 and 3:59. No need to check minutes separately.
# for example: "crimes between 10:15 PM and 3:45 AM” or "crimes after 3:30 AM”, then you need hour + minute

crimes_night = crimes[(crimes["hour"] >= 22) | (crimes["hour"] <= 3)]
crimes_night

peak_night_crime_location = crimes_night["area_name"].mode()[0]
peak_night_crime_location
Out[702]:
'Central'

Visualization Using matplotlib - Using Series/Array — Night Crime Frequency by Area¶

In [706]:
night_crime_counts = crimes_night["area_name"].value_counts()

plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))

night_crime_counts.plot(kind= "bar")

plt.title("Night Crimes Frequency by Area", fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel("Area Name", fontsize=14)
plt.ylabel("Number of Night Crimes", fontsize=14)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, fontsize=11)

plt.show()

Insight: The Central area has the highest number of crimes during nighttime hours, followed by areas such as Hollywood and 77th Street. The gradual decline across areas suggests that night crime is concentrated in specific regions rather than evenly distributed across the city.

Recommendation: Targeted interventions in high-risk areas like Central may be more effective than city-wide strategies. The concentration of nightlife activities (e.g., entertainment venues and transportation hubs) may contribute to increased exposure and crime risk during nighttime hours.

Q3) How does crime distribution vary by victim age group?¶

Define age bins and labels¶

In [712]:
bins = [0, 17, 25, 34, 44,54, 64, float("inf")]

labels = ["0-17", "18-25", "26-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+"]

Feature Engineering: Create categorical column for age groups using pd.cut()¶

In [715]:
crimes["age_group"] = pd.cut(crimes["vict_age"], bins=bins, labels=labels, right=True)

A small number of records (category "H" = 30 occurrences) appear in the dataset but are not clearly defined. Given their extremely low frequency (<0.016%), these entries are treated as data noise or inconsistencies and have minimal impact on the overall analysis.

The presence of this negligible number of ambiguous categories suggests potential data entry inconsistencies. Due to their minimal impact, these values are excluded from the analysis to improve clarity and interpretability.

The consistency between count-based and proportion-based analyses further reinforces the reliability of these findings.

Appendix — Alternative Approaches and Plots¶

Appendix 1 – Alternative Approaches Using .mode() to identify Peak Crime Hour¶

This alternative approach identifies the peak crime hour by counting occurrences of each hour and selecting the most frequent one.

In [3515]:
# mode()- returns all most frequent values as a Series
# so I use mode()[0] to extract a single value when needed. Statistically correct, handles ties.


# However, I’m aware that there can be multiple modes, so in a production scenario I would check for ties explicitly.

peak_crime_hour = crimes["hour"].mode()[0]
peak_crime_hour
Out[3515]:
12

Appendix 2 – Alternative Approaches to Identify Peak Night Crime Area¶

Method 1: Aggregation using value_counts()¶

This approach uses aggregation to count the number of crimes per area during nighttime hours and selects the area with the highest frequency.

value_counts(): counts how many crimes occurred in each area

idxmax(): returns the area (index) with the highest count

In [1681]:
# Count night crimes per area and return the most frequent
# value_counts(): counts how many crimes occurred in each area
# idxmax(): returns the area (index) with the highest count

peak_night_crime_location = crimes["area_name"].value_counts().idxmax()
peak_night_crime_location
Out[1681]:
'Central'

The result shows that the Central area has the highest number of crimes committed during nighttime hours.

Method 2: Time-based filtering using datetime¶

In [1685]:
from datetime import time

# Extract time component for precise comparison
crimes["time"] = crimes["time_occ"].dt.time

# Use OR (|) because the time range crosses midnight (22:00 → 03:59))
crimes_night = crimes[(crimes["time"] >= time(22, 0)) | (crimes["time"] <= time(3, 59))] 

# Identify most frequent area
peak_night_crime_location = crimes_night["area_name"].mode()[0]
peak_night_crime_location
Out[1685]:
'Central'

Both approaches confirm that Central has the highest number of night crimes. This consistency reinforces the validity of the filtering logic and strengthens confidence in the analysis. The concentration of crimes in this area may indicate higher nighttime activity, population density, or differences in reporting and policing across locations.

Appendix 3 – Alternative Approaches to identify the Most Affected Age Group¶

Method 1: This approach groups records by age_group and uses .size() to count the number of crimes in each category including missing values.¶

pd.cut() creates the categorical age ranges (it is used to turn a continuous numeric variable into interval-based categories.)

groupby("age_group") groups rows by those ranges

.size() counts how many crimes fall in each group,

.size() counts all rows in each group, including missing values.

Aggregation using groupby() and size()

In [141]:
# Define bins and labels
bins = [0, 17, 25, 34, 44, 54, 64, float("inf")]
labels = ["0-17", "18-25", "26-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+"]


# pd.cut() - It takes numeric values and places each value into a bin.
# Create age group column
crimes["age_group"] = pd.cut(crimes["vict_age"], bins=bins, labels=labels, include_lowest=True)


# Alternative approach using groupby()
victim_ages = crimes.groupby("age_group", observed=False).size().reindex(labels)

victim_ages

Method 2:This approach groups records by age_group and uses .count() to count only the non-null values for the number of crimes in each category.¶

pd.cut() creates the categorical age ranges (it is used to turn a continuous numeric variable into interval-based categories.)

groupby("age_group") groups rows by those ranges

.count() counts non-null values in a specific column, while .size() counts all rows.

Aggregation using groupby() and count()

})

Method 5 : Identifying the highest group using - .loc[] and .idxmax()¶

# age_df["count"].idxmax() → gives row index of max value

Final Insight¶

The 26–34 age group consistently experiences the highest number of crimes. This suggests that working-age adults are more exposed to crime, likely due to higher levels of mobility, social interaction, and time spent in public environments.

Using multiple approaches ensures that results are not dependent on a single method and increases confidence in the findings.

plt.xticks(rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()

Theft-related crimes, particularly identity theft, are the most frequent, followed by battery and assault-related offenses. This indicates that both property crimes and violent incidents play a significant role in overall crime patterns.

All methods consistently identify the same top 5 crime types, confirming the reliability and robustness of the analysis.

Final Insight: Theft-related crimes dominate the dataset, indicating that non-violent and lower-severity incidents occur more frequently than high-severity crimes. This suggests that targeted prevention strategies—such as fraud awareness and property protection—could significantly reduce overall crime levels.

Using multiple visualization approaches ensures that results are consistent and not dependent on a single plotting method.

Appendix 7 — Alternative Approach to Analyze Weekday vs Weekend Crime Distribution¶

Method: Using value_counts(normalize=True)¶

This alternative approach computes the proportion of crimes occurring on weekdays and weekends using a more concise pandas method. .map() was used to convert boolean values into meaningful categorical labels, making the data easier to interpret and visualize.

In [475]:
# isin(["Saturday", "Sunday"]) checks: If the day is Saturday or Sunday → True, Otherwise → False
crimes["day_type"] = crimes["day_of_week"].isin(["Saturday", "Sunday"])

crimes["day_type"] = crimes["day_type"].map({True: "Weekend", False: "Weekday"})

crimes["day_type"].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
